key_insight: The paper argues that RLVR does not need to completely reshape a model to improve reasoning; instead, it largely reuses the base model’s existing weight spectra while changing behavior through a smaller set of structural updates. This "spectral inheritance" helps explain how reward-driven training can be efficient and stable.
problem_solved: It addresses the poorly understood optimization layer in RLVR: how reward feedback is converted into actual weight-space updates in the model, and why these updates can improve reasoning without full-scale weight reorganization.
method: Analyze the singular structure of model weights to track how RLVR changes the spectrum of the base model.
Identify and characterize "spectral inheritance" as the reuse of pretrained weight spectra during RLVR optimization.
Study how behavior changes emerge from updates in the associative structure rather than from wholesale spectral replacement.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more interpretable view of RLVR training dynamics and may guide more efficient fine-tuning strategies for reasoning models. It can help researchers design optimization methods that preserve useful pretrained structure while enabling new capabilities.
visual_elements: Before-and-after spectrum diagram showing base model vs. RLVR-updated weight singular values
Pipeline graphic: reward signal -> optimization layer -> weight update -> improved reasoning
Annotated matrix/SVD illustration highlighting inherited vs. modified components
Side-by-side behavior comparison showing preserved general knowledge and improved reasoning outputs
paper_authors: Hanqing Zhu, Wenyan Cong, Zhizhou Sha, Sagnik Mukherjee, Xinyuan Song
